name: Aider polyglot benchmark
what_it_measures: Whole-file/diff code editing ability across six languages under a fixed two-attempt loop: solve the exercise, and if tests fail, retry once with the failing test output. Also measures edit-format compliance (can the model emit a syntactically valid diff).
task_source: 225 of Exercism's hardest exercises across C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python, Rust (launched December 2024 to replace the saturated Python-only aider benchmark).
metric: pass_rate_2 (pass rate after two attempts) as primary; 'percent cases well-formed' (edit-format compliance) and total cost per run as secondary. Top entry: gpt-5 at 88.0% (run dated 2025-08-25).
contamination_status: Weak — Exercism exercises and their solutions are public and old; the benchmark's discriminative power comes from difficulty selection and the edit-format constraint, not contamination resistance. Scores near 88% suggest approaching saturation.
maintenance_state: stale — leaderboard page last updated 2025-11-20 but newest model runs date to 2025-08-25; no 2026-generation models listed as of July 2026.
harness_lessons: The well-formed-edits metric isolates a harness-critical variable most benchmarks conflate with intelligence: whether the model can drive YOUR edit format reliably, which is often the binding constraint in an agent loop. The one-retry-with-test-output protocol is a cheap, reproducible feedback-loop design worth copying. Publishing cost per run alongside accuracy made cost-normalized comparison standard practice.
notes: Third-party trackers (llm-stats.com/benchmarks/aider-polyglot, leaderboard.steel.dev) continue rescoring newer models against the same task set, so numbers for 2026 models exist outside the official page. Benchmark repo lives inside github.com/Aider-AI/aider (benchmark/ directory).

name: Commit0
what_it_measures: From-scratch library generation: given a specification document (often hundreds of pages) and an interactive unit-test suite, rebuild 57 core Python libraries so their tests pass — long-context spec reading, multi-stage test feedback, thousands of functions with real interdependencies.
task_source: 57 real Python libraries stripped to specs + tests; lite/all splits; isolated per-library execution environments (Docker/Modal backends).
metric: Fraction of unit tests passed per library. SOTA at paper time: 17% of tests on the easier (lite) libraries, 6% across all libraries without feedback; no agent reproduces a full library.
contamination_status: Deliberately inverted — the target libraries ARE in every model's pretraining data, so the benchmark measures reconstruction from spec rather than memorization avoidance; verbatim recall of implementations is a confound the interactive-test protocol only partially controls.
maintenance_state: stale — repo (github.com/commit-0/commit0, MIT, 646 commits) last saw notable updates around late 2024 (o1 compatibility note 2024-09-28); still cited as a frontier target in 2026 papers (FeatureBench, RepoZero) because scores remain very low.
harness_lessons: Interactive test suites as the task definition (tests-as-spec) is the purest form of verifiable reward, and Commit0's distributed per-library sandboxes show the infra cost of scaling it. The gap between 17% on lite and 6% overall quantifies how fast agent competence decays with codebase size and interdependency, a decay curve worth measuring in your own harness before trusting an agent with a large repo.
notes: Useful contrast to SWE-Bench-style patching: 0-to-1 generation, not 1-to-n repair. Successor greenfield efforts: RepoZero (arXiv 2605.07122), 0-to-1 CLI-tool study (arXiv 2604.06742).

name: FeatureBench
what_it_measures: End-to-end feature development rather than bug patching: tasks span multiple commits/PRs and require implementing coherent feature-level functionality, the gap between SWE-bench-style repairs and real feature work.
task_source: 200 evaluation tasks with 3,825 executable environments from 24 open-source repositories, auto-derived by tracing unit tests along dependency graphs to identify feature-scale units of work (scalable toolkit, refreshable over time).
metric: Task resolution rate via test verification. Claude Opus 4.5 scores 11.0% vs its 74.4% on SWE-bench — a ~63-point drop on the same model.
contamination_status: Mined from public repos (exposed), but the automated collection toolkit is explicitly designed to regenerate fresh post-cutoff tasks over time, making refresh the contamination strategy rather than secrecy.
maintenance_state: active — submitted 2026-02-11, accepted ICLR 2026; first public version; refresh pipeline promised.
harness_lessons: Auto-deriving tasks from test dependency graphs is a template for building an eval from your own repo without hand-annotation, which is the only way internal benchmarks stay fresh. The 74%-to-11% collapse from bug-fix to feature-scale tasks quantifies task-granularity as the dominant difficulty variable: agent reliability numbers are meaningless without stating the size of the unit of work.
notes: Part of the 2026 wave restoring headroom after SWE-bench saturation (with SWE-Bench Pro, RoadmapBench arXiv 2605.15846, SmellBench arXiv 2606.05574, ContextBench arXiv 2602.05892). Authors: Qixing Zhou, Jiacheng Zhang, et al.

name: HAL — Holistic Agent Leaderboard
what_it_measures: Not a task set: a standardized, centralized harness for running third-party agents across many benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, USACO, AppWorld, CORE-bench, tau-bench, ...) with identical orchestration, so cross-benchmark and cross-agent numbers are comparable and cost-annotated.
task_source: Wraps existing benchmarks; validation campaign: 21,730 agent rollouts, 9 models x 9 benchmarks across coding, web, science, customer service, ~$40k total cost.
metric: Per-benchmark accuracy plus dollar cost per run (cost-accuracy Pareto frontiers), with parallel execution across hundreds of VMs.
contamination_status: Inherits each wrapped benchmark's contamination profile; its own contribution is eliminating implementation-variance confounds (harness bugs) rather than leakage control.
maintenance_state: frozen/pivoted — hal-harness repo (princeton-pli/hal-harness) archived for historical reference; the team (Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan; ICLR 2026 paper) has pivoted to the HAL Reliability Dashboard (hal.cs.princeton.edu/reliability) and the cross-org AI Evaluator Forum.
harness_lessons: Their core finding is this book's thesis in benchmark form: a shared harness 'eliminates common implementation bugs' that otherwise dominate reported differences between agents, and evaluation cost (~$40k for one validation sweep) is a first-class engineering constraint. The pivot from leaderboard to reliability dashboard is the field's measurement frontier moving from 'how capable' to 'how consistently', the exact framing of Part Measurement.
notes: Cite alongside Inspect (UK AISI) and Harbor as the three public reference harnesses of 2025-2026. Cost-of-evals context: huggingface.co/blog/evaleval/eval-costs-bottleneck; 'Efficient Benchmarking of AI Agents' arXiv 2603.23749.

name: LiveCodeBench
what_it_measures: Four code capabilities beyond generation: code generation, self-repair, code execution (predict behavior without running), and test-output prediction, evaluated as a function of problem release date to expose contamination.
task_source: Problems continuously scraped from LeetCode, AtCoder, and Codeforces contests, tagged with release dates. Rolling versions: v1 400 problems (May 2023-Mar 2024) through v6 1055 problems (May 2023-Apr 2025).
metric: pass@1 (and pass@5) against hidden test cases, sliceable by time window so models are scored only on problems released after their training cutoff.
contamination_status: Contamination-aware by construction — the date-windowing design is the whole point; performance drop-off on post-cutoff windows is used as a leakage detector. Requires trusting vendor-declared cutoffs.
maintenance_state: active — GitHub repo maintained with dataset expansions through 2025 (v6 = Apr 2025 window); third-party leaderboards (artificialanalysis.ai, benchlm.ai) rescore 2026 models on it; official version cadence has slowed relative to 2024.
harness_lessons: Date-stamping every task and slicing metrics by time window is the cheapest robust contamination control available, and it transfers directly to internal eval suites built from your own issue history. Measuring self-repair and execution-prediction separately from generation shows how to decompose 'coding ability' into the sub-skills your harness actually exercises.
notes: Distinct from LiveBench (livebench.ai) and from LiveCodeBench Pro (separate team/card). Hugging Face leaderboard: huggingface.co/blog/leaderboard-livecodebench. GitHub: github.com/LiveCodeBench/LiveCodeBench.

name: LiveCodeBench Pro
what_it_measures: Olympiad-grade algorithmic reasoning with expert diagnosis: every failed submission is analyzed line-by-line by Olympiad medalists who classify errors as idea-level vs implementation-level, giving causal failure diagnostics instead of a bare pass rate.
task_source: 584 problems (as of 2025-04-25) from Codeforces, ICPC, IOI, and select university contests, continuously updated; problems captured before public editorials/solutions exist.
metric: pass@1 stratified by difficulty tier plus expert error taxonomy. At paper time the best model hit 53% on medium problems and 0% on hard; models proved implementation-strong but reasoning-weak, with confidently incorrect justifications.
contamination_status: Strong — continuous ingestion of fresh contest problems before editorials circulate; explicit contamination controls are a design pillar.
maintenance_state: active — NeurIPS 2025 paper, continuously updated problem feed; separate team from original LiveCodeBench (Zheng, Cheng et al., NYU-affiliated).
harness_lessons: The medalist annotation layer demonstrates that WHY an agent failed (idea vs implementation) is a different, more actionable measurement than whether it failed, and pure pass/fail leaderboards systematically hide the difference. For harness builders: budget for human (or strong-model) failure triage on a sample of runs; the idea/implementation split is a reusable taxonomy for agent transcript autopsies.
notes: Name collides with but is independent of LiveCodeBench; treat as a hard-ceiling reasoning benchmark rather than an agentic/terminal one. Hugging Face paper page: huggingface.co/papers/2506.11928.

name: METR Task-Completion Time Horizons (TH1.1)
what_it_measures: The human task length at which a model succeeds 50% of the time (the 50% time horizon), fitted across a suite of software/research tasks with known human completion times — a capability trend line rather than a leaderboard.
task_source: TH1.1 (2026-01-29): 228 tasks (up from 170; +73 HCAST tasks added, 15 removed, 53 updated), drawn from HCAST, RE-Bench, and SWAA short tasks; long tasks (8h+) doubled to 31; runs on UK AISI's open-source Inspect framework (migrated off in-house Vivaria).
metric: 50% (and 80%) task-completion time horizon in human-minutes, plus doubling time of the trend. TH1.1: doubling 131 days since 2023, 89 days since 2024 (vs original 7 months). Horizons: Claude Opus 4.5 = 320 min; GPT-5 = 214 min; later 2026 reporting puts Claude Opus 4.6 near 719 min.
contamination_status: Tasks are mostly private/bespoke (HCAST/RE-Bench held by METR), so leakage is low; main validity threats are task-suite composition drift and the human-baseline time estimates, both explicitly versioned in the 1.1 methodology update.
maintenance_state: active — Time Horizon 1.1 released 2026-01-29; public data at github.com/METR/eval-analysis-public; tracked externally by Epoch AI and theaidigest.org.
harness_lessons: Expressing capability in human-time units is the most communicable metric yet invented for agent evals, and it transfers: baseline your internal tasks with human completion times and you get an org-local time-horizon curve. The 1.0-to-1.1 revision shows mature practice for versioning a benchmark whose task suite must grow (publish the diff: added/removed/updated task counts and the effect on the trend). Migration to Inspect signals consolidation onto shared open-source eval infrastructure.
notes: The 50%-horizon is a median, not a reliability guarantee; METR's own data shows 80%-horizons are roughly 4-5x shorter, which is the number that matters for unattended production use. Doubling-time discourse (4.3 vs 7 months) is sensitive to fit window — cite the window with the number.

name: MLE-bench
what_it_measures: Autonomous machine-learning engineering: train models, prepare data, and run experiments to medal in real Kaggle competitions, under a standardized compute budget (24h, 36 vCPU, 440GB RAM, one 24GB GPU).
task_source: 75 curated Kaggle competitions across 15 problem categories; complexity tiers: 22 low (<2h for an experienced engineer, the 'Lite' split), 38 medium (2-10h), 15 high (>10h); human baselines from public Kaggle leaderboards.
metric: 'Any Medal' rate (% of competitions where the agent's CSV submission clears a medal threshold), mean ± SE over ≥3 seeds. Launch SOTA: o1-preview + AIDE scaffolding at 16.9%; leaderboard entries through Feb 2026 range 1.60%-77.78% on full.
contamination_status: Known weakness — competitions and winning solutions are public and heavily discussed; OpenAI documents 13 known task issues and plans batched v2 fixes via openai/frontier-evals. Medal thresholds vs historical leaderboards partially mitigate but do not remove leakage.
maintenance_state: active-but-paused — as of February 2026 the leaderboard is closed to new submissions while OpenAI builds 'an improved process for ensuring submissions are fair and comparable'; v2 planned under openai/frontier-evals.
harness_lessons: The Feb 2026 submission freeze is the key artifact: even a well-resourced maintainer found self-reported agent results incomparable without a standardized execution harness, which is the strongest public argument for running evals yourself rather than trusting leaderboard PRs. Fixed compute budgets and ≥3-seed reporting with standard error are baseline hygiene any internal agent eval should copy.
notes: Scaffolding (AIDE vs others) moves scores as much as model choice, an early public demonstration of harness-dominates-model. OECD.AI catalogue entry: oecd.ai/en/catalogue/tools/mle-bench.

name: Multi-SWE-bench
what_it_measures: SWE-bench-style issue resolution beyond Python: 2,132 expert-curated instances across Python, Java, TypeScript, JavaScript, Go, Rust, C, and C++, exposing how much of reported agent skill is Python monoculture.
task_source: Real GitHub issues/PRs across 8 languages, filtered and validated by 68 expert annotators (ByteDance Seed); subsets: mini (400 instances, Apr 2025) and flash (300 instances, Jul 2025) for cheap evaluation; companion Multi-SWE-RL community dataset (4,723 instances) for RL training.
metric: Resolve rate per language (patch passes the repo's tests), typically reported with a large Python-vs-rest gap.
contamination_status: Same exposure as all mined-from-GitHub benchmarks — instances are public history; language diversity does not itself protect against leakage, and no held-out split exists.
maintenance_state: active — flash subset released Jul 2025, Multi-SWE-RL community ongoing; dataset on Hugging Face (ByteDance-Seed/Multi-SWE-bench); referenced by 2026 successors like SWE-Compass.
harness_lessons: Per-language resolve-rate gaps are a proxy for how your harness will degrade on the parts of your stack that are not Python; measure per-language before assuming benchmark numbers transfer. The mini/flash subset strategy (400/300 instances) is the practical answer to eval cost: a stratified small split for the inner loop, the full set for releases. The RL-dataset companion shows benchmarks now double as training-data factories, which accelerates their own contamination.
notes: Complements Aider polyglot (editing-level) at the issue-resolution level. Eight-language coverage makes it the standard non-Python citation in 2026 model cards.

name: RepoBench
what_it_measures: Repository-level auto-completion decomposed into three tasks: RepoBench-R (retrieve the right cross-file context), RepoBench-C (complete the next line given context), RepoBench-P (end-to-end retrieval+completion pipeline), in Python and Java.
task_source: GitHub repositories; v1.1 (released 2024-02-05) sources repos created 2023-10-06 through 2023-12-31 to post-date training cutoffs of the era; masked-line settings: cross-file-first, cross-file-random, in-file.
metric: Exact Match, Edit Similarity, and CodeBLEU on the masked line, reported across context-window levels.
contamination_status: Time-windowed at release (post-cutoff repos for 2023-era models), but the window is now inside every current model's training data; treat all absolute numbers as contaminated for 2025-2026 models.
maintenance_state: frozen — v1.1 (Feb 2024, ICLR 2024) is the last release; archive/v0 branch kept for paper reproduction; no 2025-2026 data refresh. Successor niche filled by SecRepoBench, ContextBench (arXiv 2602.05892), SaraCoder-style work.
harness_lessons: Splitting retrieval from completion (R vs C vs P) is the right decomposition for debugging context engineering: when the pipeline fails you know whether retrieval or generation lost the thread, which maps directly onto agent context-assembly design. Its decay also illustrates the maintenance treadmill: a time-windowed benchmark without a refresh pipeline has a shelf life of roughly one model generation.
notes: Predates agentic evals; still the standard citation for completion-with-cross-file-context. Data on Hugging Face (Repobench Python/Java V1.1). Interesting mostly as a cautionary tale plus a clean task taxonomy for Part Measurement.

name: SlopCodeBench (SCBench)
what_it_measures: Code-quality degradation as an agent extends its OWN solution through successive requirement changes: correctness at each checkpoint plus two lower-is-better slop axes, Erosion (complexity/redundancy accumulating in already-complex code) and Verbosity (bloat).
task_source: 36 iterative problems / 196 checkpoints authored for the benchmark (SprocketLab); black-box design: agents get only CLI/API contracts, no prescribed architecture, so early design decisions compound across checkpoints.
metric: Isolated solve rate (top performers 16.3-28.1%; v1.0 leader GPT-5.5/Codex at 28.1%), plus Erosion and Verbosity scores 0-1 (lower better; leader erosion 0.494) judged by an LLM rubric. Across 11 models in the paper, no agent solves a problem end-to-end; verbosity rises in 90% of trajectories, erosion in 80%.
contamination_status: Purpose-written tasks, low pretraining-leakage risk; the LLM-judge component introduces judge-model dependence rather than test-set leakage as the main validity concern.
maintenance_state: active — v1.0 leaderboard live at scbench.ai with 19 models as of July 2026; paper (arXiv 2603.24755, 2026); backed by Snorkel AI, DARPA, NSF; positioned as a community-driven evaluation primitive, not a frozen set.
harness_lessons: The single benchmark that measures the failure mode most production harnesses hit: agents pass today's checkpoint by eroding tomorrow's codebase, so a harness gating only on tests green will accumulate slop invisibly. Checkpointed re-evaluation of earlier functionality (their broken-while-extending signal) belongs in any long-lived agent loop. Semantic quality judgments are delegated to an LLM judge rather than static metrics, which is the same ZFC boundary a harness should respect.
notes: Direct ancestor of this project's /slop-check skill and anti-slop rules. Snorkel mirror: snorkel.ai/leaderboard/slopcode-bench/. GitHub: github.com/SprocketLab/slop-code-bench.

name: SWE-bench
what_it_measures: Whether an LM/agent can resolve real GitHub issues in mature Python repositories by producing a patch that passes previously-failing tests without breaking passing ones.
task_source: 2,294 issue+PR pairs mined from 12 popular Python repositories (django, sympy, scikit-learn, etc.), each with a gold patch and fail-to-pass / pass-to-pass test sets.
metric: % resolved (patch makes all FAIL_TO_PASS tests pass while all PASS_TO_PASS tests still pass), evaluated in Dockerized per-instance environments.
contamination_status: Heavily contaminated. All tasks predate 2023 model cutoffs; SWE-Bench+ (arXiv:2410.06992) found ~32.67% of "resolved" instances had solution leakage in issue text and ~47.93% passed only because of weak tests; OpenAI's June 2026 audit found frontier models trained on benchmark solutions.
maintenance_state: active (tooling) / frozen (dataset). The swebench pip package is maintained (pypi swebench 1.0.13) and swebench.com leaderboards still run as of July 2026, but the full 2,294-task split is effectively superseded by Verified/Pro/Live for reporting.
harness_lessons: The FAIL_TO_PASS + PASS_TO_PASS dual-oracle is the canonical pattern for repo-level eval - a fix must both solve the problem and not regress anything, and you should copy that discipline into any internal harness. Pre-1.0 SWE-bench had notorious reproducibility drift (results varied with host environment) until full Docker containerization; environment pinning is not optional. The weak-test findings show "tests pass" is only as strong as the tests - audit your oracle before trusting your resolve rate.
notes: Progenitor of the entire family; the ecosystem (SWE-agent, mini-SWE-agent, SWE-ReX, SWE-smith, sb-cli) lives under the SWE-bench GitHub org. Original leaderboard splits: full, Lite, Verified, Multimodal, Multilingual.

name: SWE-bench Lite
what_it_measures: Same issue-resolution capability as SWE-bench, on a 300-instance subset curated for cheaper, faster evaluation (filtered toward self-contained, mostly single-file bug fixes with clearer issue descriptions).
task_source: 300 instances subsampled from the original 2,294 Python tasks (11 repos), filtered to remove instances with images/links, very large diffs, and underspecified issues.
metric: % resolved (same FAIL_TO_PASS / PASS_TO_PASS oracle as parent).
contamination_status: Same as parent - contaminated; SWE-Bench+ TestEnhancer work showed strengthening Lite's tests dropped resolution rates ~27 percentage points on average, i.e. a large fraction of "resolved" Lite instances passed on weak tests.
maintenance_state: active leaderboard / frozen dataset. Third-party leaderboards still update (e.g. pricepertoken.com shows Claude Opus 4.6 at 62.7 on July 20, 2026) but the split is no longer where frontier progress is reported.
harness_lessons: Subsampling for cost changes what you measure - Lite's filters systematically skew toward easier, single-file fixes, so a Lite score is not a scaled-down full-bench score. When you build a "smoke suite" subset of your own evals, document the selection filters and expect a difficulty shift. Cheap subsets are for iteration speed, not for headline claims.
notes: The de facto dev-loop split during 2024; most agent papers of that era iterated on Lite. Its selection-bias story is a useful teaching example for internal eval design.

name: SWE-bench-Live
family: SWE-bench descendant (Microsoft Research + collaborators, NeurIPS 2025 D&B)
what_it_measures: Issue resolution on continuously refreshed, recent GitHub issues - capability measurement designed to stay ahead of training cutoffs rather than freeze a split.
task_source: Initial release: 1,319 tasks from issues created since 2024 across 93 repositories, curated by an automated pipeline. RepoLaunch (arXiv:2603.05026), an LLM agent, builds the containerized test environment for any repo; the Feb 2026 upgrade extended it to all mainstream languages (C, C++, C#, Python, Java, Go, JS/TS, Rust) on both Linux and Windows.
metric: % resolved on rolling monthly splits; instances validated by running regression tests three times to filter flaky/invalid tasks.
contamination_status: Structurally decontaminated by recency - tasks postdate model cutoffs at evaluation time and the split rolls forward. Trade-off: higher week-to-week variance than frozen splits, and repos themselves remain in training corpora (only the specific issue/patch pairs are fresh).
maintenance_state: active (June 2026: added MIT-IBM BOAD and Brokk Agent results, GPT-5.5 and DeepSeek-v4-Pro evaluated per-language; monthly task additions ongoing).
harness_lessons: Automated environment provisioning is the scaling bottleneck for any live eval - RepoLaunch demonstrates you need an agent to build the harness before an agent can be tested in it. Triple-run regression filtering is a concrete flakiness gate worth copying: an instance whose oracle is not deterministic across three runs is not an eval instance. Rolling splits trade comparability-over-time for contamination resistance; pin cohort dates in every reported number.
notes: The "evergreen benchmark" archetype. Compare with SWE-rebench and SWE-MERA, which reach the same design point independently.

name: SWE-bench Multilingual
paper_url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770 (extension by the SWE-bench team; released with mini-SWE-agent work, May 2025)
what_it_measures: Issue resolution beyond Python: whether agents and harnesses generalize across language ecosystems, build systems, and test frameworks.
task_source: 300 task instances across 9 languages (JavaScript, TypeScript, C, C++, Go, Java, PHP, Ruby, Rust) from 42 GitHub repositories spanning web frameworks, data tools, core utilities, and libraries.
metric: % resolved (FAIL_TO_PASS / PASS_TO_PASS, per-language containerized environments).
contamination_status: Same structural exposure as the Python splits (public repos, public gold patches); mitigated only by being newer and less used as training-target than Verified. No formal contamination audit published.
maintenance_state: active (official swebench.com leaderboard as of July 2026; third-party mirrors like llm-stats track it).
harness_lessons: Most of the engineering cost of going multilingual is environment construction, not agent logic - nine languages means nine build/test toolchains to containerize deterministically. Per-language resolve-rate spreads reveal which parts of your harness silently assume Python (test discovery, trace parsing, patch application). If your production agents work in a polyglot monorepo, a Python-only eval overstates reliability.
notes: The official team's answer to Multi-SWE-bench; smaller (300 vs 1,632 instances) but integrated into the standard swebench tooling.

name: SWE-bench Multimodal (SWE-bench M)
what_it_measures: Whether agents can fix bugs in visual, user-facing JavaScript software when the problem statement or tests contain images (screenshots, rendered output, diagrams).
task_source: 617 task instances from 17 JavaScript libraries (web UI, diagramming, data visualization, syntax highlighting, interactive mapping); every instance has at least one image in the issue or unit tests.
metric: % resolved via hidden test suites; test split held private, submissions run through sb-cli cloud evaluation.
contamination_status: Better-protected than the Python splits - the test split is private and evaluation is centralized, so gold patches for the eval set are not sitting in public training corpora. Task repos themselves are public.
maintenance_state: active (integrated into the SWE-bench repo January 2025; leaderboard maintained at swebench.com as of July 2026).
harness_lessons: A private eval split plus centralized cloud grading (sb-cli) is the family's first structural contamination control - the pattern to copy when you must publish a benchmark but keep the oracle. It also exposed harness overfitting: Python-specialized scaffolds collapsed on JavaScript, while SWE-agent's language-agnostic design resolved 12% vs 6% for the next best system - a direct measurement of how much "agent capability" is actually harness specialization. Budget for asset plumbing: images in issues break text-only context pipelines.
notes: First family member to force multimodal context handling. Initial resolve rates (~12%) versus contemporaneous ~40-50% on Verified quantified the generalization gap.

name: SWE-Bench+ (SWE-bench+)
family: SWE-bench descendant / audit (York University et al., Oct 2024)
what_it_measures: Primarily an audit of SWE-bench validity, plus a cleaned dataset: issue resolution on instances free of solution leakage and (in later revisions) with strengthened test suites.
task_source: Re-analysis of SWE-bench agent runs plus a refreshed instance set collected from PRs created after model training cutoffs, filtered for solution leakage. Later versions add SolutionLeakDetector (LLM leak filter, 80.45% detection accuracy) and TestEnhancer (LLM test strengthening, improved patch validation for 97.11% of weak-test issues).
metric: % resolved, after leak filtering and test augmentation; headline finding is the delta versus original SWE-bench scores.
contamination_status: This IS the contamination paper: found 32.67% of SWE-agent+GPT-4 "resolved" instances had the solution in the issue text (60.83% in one analyzed slice including hints in comments) and 47.93% passed only due to weak tests; resolution rates dropped ~27 points on Lite after test enhancement. Its own cleaned set ages back into contamination as cutoffs advance.
maintenance_state: stale (research artifact; no live leaderboard; last substantive update the 2025 OpenReview revision cycle).
harness_lessons: Run a leakage audit on your own task corpus before believing pass rates - if the answer is in the prompt context (issue text, comments, linked PRs), you are measuring retrieval, not engineering. Weak oracles inflate scores silently; an LLM-based test-strengthening pass is cheap relative to the cost of shipping decisions made on inflated numbers. Deltas before/after cleaning are themselves the most informative metric a harness can emit.
notes: The paper that forced the family's contamination reckoning two years before OpenAI's 2026 retraction of Verified. Distinct from SWE-Bench++ (arXiv:2512.17419), a different group's generation framework.

name: SWE-Bench++
what_it_measures: Both a framework and a corpus: automated generation of repository-level coding tasks (bug fixes AND features) from real GitHub PRs across many languages, evaluating models on a much broader, continuously extensible task distribution than hand-curated splits.
task_source: 11,133 instances from 3,971 repositories across 11 programming languages, produced by a four-stage pipeline - programmatic sourcing, environment synthesis, test oracle extraction, quality assurance - plus a trajectory-synthesis stage that converts hard instances into training data.
metric: pass@k on extracted test oracles; on a 1,782-instance benchmark slice: Claude Sonnet 4.5 36.20% pass@10, GPT-5 34.57%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 24.92%, GPT-4o 16.89%.
contamination_status: Mined from public PRs (same leakage class as classic SWE-bench), but the generation pipeline can re-run on fresh history, making decontamination an operational choice rather than a dataset property.
maintenance_state: active-young (Dec 2025 release; watch adoption - it competes with SWE-bench-Live/rebench pipelines and Scale's Pro for the "successor" slot).
harness_lessons: Treating the benchmark as the output of a pipeline, not a dataset, is the endpoint of the family's evolution - environment synthesis and test-oracle extraction are the two stages that consume nearly all engineering effort, matching RepoLaunch's lesson. Feature-implementation tasks (not just bug fixes) widen the measured distribution toward real backlog work. The built-in hard-instance-to-training-data stage shows how quickly any public eval now becomes training signal; assume your published benchmark has a half-life measured in months.
notes: Name collision hazard: distinct from SWE-Bench+ (arXiv:2410.06992, the contamination audit). Cite by arXiv ID to disambiguate.

name: SWE-Bench Pro
what_it_measures: Long-horizon issue resolution on professional codebases, designed to restore headroom after SWE-bench Verified saturation: harder multi-file tasks, regression checks, and a standardized 250-turn agent loop.
task_source: 1,865 tasks from 41 professional repositories in three subsets: public (731, exclusively GPL/copyleft repos), private commercial (276, startup codebases, never released), held-out (858, for future analysis).
metric: Resolve rate: patch passes fail-to-pass tests AND introduces no regressions on existing tests. Top models ~23% on the public set (vs 70%+ for the same models on SWE-bench Verified).
contamination_status: Strongest contamination design in the SWE-bench family: GPL licensing as a legal deterrent to training-set inclusion, a never-published commercial split, and a held-out set that never touches the public leaderboard.
maintenance_state: active — Scale AI leaderboard live and updated through 2026; identical tooling and turn limits enforced across all entrants.
harness_lessons: The 70%-to-23% collapse on the same models is the cleanest public measurement of benchmark-specific overfitting, and the reason to keep a private task set for any harness you tune. The dual gate (fix verified by fail-to-pass tests, no regressions on the existing suite) is the correct acceptance criterion for production agent patches; single-test grading overstates competence. Running every model through identical scaffolding with a hard turn cap is what makes the numbers comparable at all.
notes: Three-tier public/commercial/held-out structure is becoming the template (cf. FeatureBench refresh pipelines). Position paper context: 'Coding Benchmarks Are Misaligned with Agentic Software Engineering' (arXiv 2606.17799).

name: SWE-bench Verified
what_it_measures: Issue resolution on a 500-instance subset where 93 professional developers screened out underspecified issues and unfair tests, intended as a cleaner signal of real capability than the full split.
task_source: 500 instances filtered from original SWE-bench Python tasks via paid human annotation of issue clarity and test fairness.
metric: % resolved (FAIL_TO_PASS / PASS_TO_PASS).
contamination_status: Compromised, per its own co-creator. OpenAI's June 2026 post "Why SWE-bench Verified no longer measures frontier coding capabilities": a 6-engineer audit of the 138 problems o3 failed across 64 runs found 59.4% had material test-design or problem-description defects (35.5% over-narrow tests, 18.8% tests requiring unspecified functionality), plus evidence that frontier models (GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash) trained on benchmark solutions. As of June 16, 2026, 99 of 100 leaderboard entries were self-reported, and the same models score materially lower on a standardized harness.
maintenance_state: frozen dataset; leaderboards still tick (BenchLM July 2026: Claude Opus 5 at 96%, top models clustered within ~1 point) but the benchmark is saturated and OpenAI recommends reporting SWE-bench Pro instead.
harness_lessons: Human verification improves a benchmark but cannot future-proof it - contamination and saturation arrive anyway, so plan benchmark retirement criteria from day one. The self-reported vs standardized-harness gap (99/100 self-reported entries) is the clearest public demonstration that scaffold and harness choices move scores as much as models do; never compare numbers produced by different harnesses. When top scores cluster within a point, remaining deltas are mostly noise plus unsolvable-task artifacts, not capability.
notes: The headline coding benchmark of 2024-2025, now the canonical cautionary tale for Part Measurement: verified != valid forever. Its rise and retirement bracket almost exactly two years.

name: SWE-EVO
what_it_measures: Long-horizon software evolution rather than point fixes: implementing version-to-version feature sets derived from release notes, requiring sustained multi-file reasoning across an entire upgrade.
task_source: 48 instances built from release notes of seven mature open-source Python projects; each task averages modifications across 21 files, validated against test suites averaging 874 tests.
metric: Fix Rate - a partial-progress metric over the validation suite, acknowledging that agents rarely complete a full evolution task; headline: GPT-5.4 with OpenHands scores ~25% on SWE-EVO versus 72.80% (GPT-5.2) on SWE-bench Verified.
contamination_status: Release notes and target versions are public history, so memorization pressure exists; the sheer task span (21 files, hundreds of tests) makes verbatim leakage less decisive than on single-patch tasks. No live refresh.
maintenance_state: active (young; revisions through May 2026, small task count, growing citation as the "long-horizon gap" reference).
harness_lessons: When tasks stop being atomic, binary resolved/unresolved wastes the signal - a partial-credit metric like Fix Rate is what makes week-long agent runs measurable, and internal harnesses for epic-scale work need the same. The 72.8%-to-25% cliff on the same model class quantifies how little short-horizon benchmarks predict sustained multi-file work; context management and plan persistence, not patch synthesis, become the failure modes. 48 instances is enough to expose a capability cliff but not to rank models closely - mind the n.
notes: The measurement-layer counterpart of the book's harness-engineering thesis: horizon length is the axis where current agents break, echoing METR's time-horizon framing.

name: SWE-fficiency
family: SWE-bench descendant / performance optimization (Nov 2025; popularized via OpenHands, Feb 2026)
what_it_measures: Repository-level performance engineering on real workloads: given a full codebase and a slow workload, the agent must localize the bottleneck, find the relevant tests, and patch to match or exceed the expert's speedup without breaking correctness.
task_source: 498 tasks across 9 heavily-used data-science/ML/HPC repositories (numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, etc.), each paired with a real slow workload and the expert's historical optimization.
metric: Speedup ratio (SR) relative to expert speedup, gated on passing the same unit tests. Headline finding: frontier LMs average under 0.23x of expert speedup and frequently introduce correctness bugs.
contamination_status: Expert patches are public repo history, but the workload-grounded runtime oracle means regurgitation only pays if it genuinely reproduces the speedup in the harness environment; no rolling refresh, so it will age.
maintenance_state: active (leaderboard/site live; OpenReview cycle and OpenHands promotion through Feb 2026).
harness_lessons: Grounding measurement in workloads ("make this slow thing fast") rather than test deltas is the closest public analogue to real performance tickets, and it demands harness-side instrumentation discipline: pinned hardware, repeated timing runs, and statistical acceptance thresholds. The 0.23x-of-expert result is a reminder to normalize agent performance against human baselines, not against zero. Agents prefer superficial micro-speedups over principled fixes - your acceptance gate must check where the speedup came from, not just that it exists.
notes: With SWE-Perf, defines the "beyond correctness" axis of the family. The 2607.01211 reliability critique applies to both.

name: SWE-Gym
family: SWE-bench descendant / training environment (UC Berkeley, UIUC, CMU, Apple; ICML 2025)
what_it_measures: Not an eval - the first public training environment for SWE agents: real tasks with executable runtimes and expert-validated unit tests, used to fine-tune agents and train verifiers whose gains are then measured on SWE-bench Verified/Lite.
task_source: 2,438 real-world Python task instances from merged PRs across 11 popular repositories deliberately disjoint from SWE-bench's 12, each with a pre-configured executable environment, natural-language task, and unit tests.
metric: Downstream: resolve-rate gains on SWE-bench Verified/Lite (up to +19% absolute from fine-tuning; 32.0%/26.0% with trained verifiers doing best-of-n over sampled trajectories).
contamination_status: N/A as an eval (it is training data by design); its repo-disjointness from SWE-bench is the load-bearing property - train/eval separation at repository granularity, not instance granularity.
maintenance_state: frozen (research artifact, ICML 2025); still widely used as an RL/SFT substrate in 2026 agent-training papers (e.g. Agent-RLVR, SkyRL lineage).
harness_lessons: Executable environments with real test oracles are what turn a benchmark harness into a reward signal - the same infrastructure serves eval and training, so build it once and keep the splits apart. Repo-level (not instance-level) train/test separation is the minimum honest boundary; instance-level splits within a repo leak project conventions and test idioms. Verifiers trained on agent trajectories give test-time scaling on top of a fixed agent - a harness feature, not a model feature.
notes: Marks the family's pivot from measuring agents to manufacturing them; SWE-smith then industrialized the idea.

name: SWE-Lancer
what_it_measures: Whether models can earn real freelance revenue: 1,400+ actual Upwork software tasks (largely on the Expensify open-source app) worth $1M total, spanning $50 bug fixes to $32,000 features, plus SWE-Manager tasks where the model picks the best implementation proposal against the real hiring manager's choice.
task_source: Real paid Upwork jobs with real payouts; IC SWE tasks graded by triple-verified end-to-end tests written by professional engineers; managerial tasks graded against ground-truth decisions.
metric: Total dollars earned (payout-weighted success), alongside per-class pass rates. Frontier models at release could not solve the majority of IC tasks; Diamond is the open reproducible split (unified Docker).
contamination_status: Moderate — Expensify's repo and issue history are public, so task material may be in training data; end-to-end-test grading (rather than the original patch) and payout weighting reduce but do not eliminate the risk.
maintenance_state: stale — dataset fixed at release (Feb 2025); Diamond split still used for cross-model comparison in 2026 but no task refresh; OpenAI's eval attention moved to frontier-evals consolidation.
harness_lessons: Dollar-weighting turns an eval into an economics statement, which is what enterprise accountability conversations actually need; the same trick works internally by weighting tasks by ticket value or engineer-hours. End-to-end tests (drive the app, not diff the patch) grade outcomes rather than similarity to a reference solution, so novel-but-correct approaches score, at the cost of much heavier verification infrastructure.
notes: The SWE-Manager half is an underused measurement of judgment (choose between proposals), distinct from generation, and close to what orchestrator agents do all day. IC-Diamond is the commonly-cited subset in 2026 model cards.

name: SWE-MERA
family: SWE-bench descendant / dynamic benchmark (MERA ecosystem, July 2025)
what_it_measures: Agentic issue resolution on a dynamic, continuously collected task stream, built explicitly to sidestep data contamination via automated collection of fresh GitHub issues with rigorous quality validation.
task_source: Automated mining pipeline yielding ~10,000 potential tasks, with 728 validated samples available at launch, drawn from issues created September 2024 - June 2025; monthly refresh intent.
metric: % resolved on time-sliced task cohorts; launch paper reports a dozen recent LLMs evaluated per cohort.
contamination_status: Decontamination-by-recency, same strategy as SWE-bench-Live and SWE-rebench: task creation dates are tracked so each model can be evaluated on post-cutoff cohorts.
maintenance_state: active-uncertain (paper revised through 2025; smaller community footprint than Live/rebench - verify current cadence before citing 2026 cohorts).
harness_lessons: The ~10,000-candidates-to-728-validated funnel is the honest number in the paper: over 90% of automatically mined tasks fail execution-based quality validation, which is the attrition rate you should expect when building your own mined eval. Time-sliced cohorts make score trends interpretable (same model, successive months) in a way frozen splits cannot. A third team independently converging on rolling decontaminated collection confirms it as the post-2025 default design.
notes: From the MERA (Russian LLM evaluation) consortium; less cited in Western leaderboard culture, useful as independent replication of the live-benchmark design point.

name: SWE-Perf
family: SWE-bench descendant / performance optimization (TikTok et al., July 2025)
what_it_measures: The first repository-level code performance-optimization benchmark: can a model make real codebases measurably faster while staying correct, rather than merely fixing bugs.
task_source: 140 curated instances derived from performance-improving PRs in popular GitHub repositories; each ships the codebase, target functions, performance-related tests, the expert patch, and an executable environment.
metric: Measured runtime improvement on performance tests, gated on correctness (unit tests still pass), compared against the expert patch's gain; evaluated for both file-level (Agentless-style) and repo-level (OpenHands-style) methods.
contamination_status: Mined from public PRs, so the expert optimization is public history; the measured-runtime oracle resists memorization somewhat (reciting the patch still has to actually run faster in the harness environment).
maintenance_state: stale-to-frozen (dataset fixed at 140 instances; repo maintained but no rolling additions as of mid-2026).
harness_lessons: A performance oracle forces your harness to control what correctness oracles ignore: hardware variance, warm-up, and repeated trials - wall-clock flakiness is the new test flakiness, and 2026 follow-up work (arXiv:2607.01211, "Are Performance-Optimization Benchmarks Reliably Measuring Coding Agents?") shows perf benchmarks are measurement-noise-sensitive. Dual gating (correct AND faster) is the template for any non-functional requirement: security, memory, cost. Expert-patch-relative scoring anchors "how good is good" to a human baseline instead of an arbitrary threshold.
notes: Revealed a substantial gap between LLMs and expert optimization. Compare SWE-fficiency (498 tasks, workload-grounded speedup ratio) - same axis, larger scale, harsher findings.

name: SWE-rebench
what_it_measures: Agentic issue resolution on a continuously mined, decontaminated task stream; doubles as a large-scale training corpus for SWE LLMs.
task_source: 21,000+ issue-PR pairs mined from 3,400+ Python repositories via a fully automated pipeline: LLM-driven extraction and validation of environment setup instructions, automated execution-based validation, and LLM-based quality annotation (clarity, complexity, test-patch validity labels per task).
metric: % resolved on fresh monthly evaluation slices; leaderboard at swe-rebench.com (July 21, 2026: Claude Opus 4.6 leads at 65.3%, GLM-5 62.8%, GLM-5.1 62.7% per BenchLM mirror).
contamination_status: Explicitly managed rather than claimed: every task carries creation dates, and evaluations that include issues predating a model's release are marked as potentially contaminated directly on the leaderboard.
maintenance_state: active (continuous collection; leaderboard updating through July 2026).
harness_lessons: Date-stamping every task against model release dates turns contamination from a binary accusation into a per-cell annotation - the most honest disclosure pattern in the family and trivially copyable in an internal eval ledger. LLM-automated task quality grading (clarity/complexity labels) shows how to scale curation without 68 human annotators. The same pipeline serving both training data and eval requires strict temporal separation - the design makes that discipline visible.
notes: Nebius also uses the corpus for RL training; the eval is the temporally-held-out tip of a training-data iceberg.

name: SWE-smith
family: SWE-bench descendant / synthetic task factory (SWE-bench team, NeurIPS 2025 D&B Spotlight)
what_it_measures: Not an eval - a toolkit that turns any GitHub repository into a "SWE-gym": it synthesizes unlimited task instances (bug injection, file localization, program repair, SWE-bench-style fixes) with executable validation, for training SWE agents at scale.
task_source: Released corpus: 52k synthetic task instances over 250+ repository environments (one Docker image per repo), plus 26k SWE-agent trajectories; 5k of those trained SWE-agent-LM-32B to 40.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified.
metric: Downstream resolve rates of models trained on its data; the toolkit itself is measured by task-generation yield per repo.
contamination_status: Synthetic bugs avoid mined-PR leakage (the "solution" never existed in public history), but generated tasks inherit distributional narrowness - agents can overfit to the injector's bug taxonomy.
maintenance_state: active (maintained under the SWE-bench GitHub org through 2026; the team's standard answer to training-data scarcity).
harness_lessons: Inverting the scarcity - generating tasks from your own codebase instead of mining public history - is the most direct route to a domain-specific, contamination-free internal benchmark; the one-Docker-image-per-repo convention keeps it operable. Synthetic bug injection gives you unlimited instances but a biased difficulty distribution; calibrate against a small mined/human set before trusting absolute numbers. Trajectory capture during training runs is free eval data for verifier models.
notes: Pairs with SWE-Gym as the "manufacture your own gym" chapter; directly applicable pattern for readers building private evals on proprietary code.

name: Terminal-Bench (1.0 / 2.0 / 2.1) + Harbor
what_it_measures: End-to-end autonomous task completion in a real command-line environment: compiling code, training models, server setup, sysadmin, security, and data-science workflows inside Docker sandboxes. 2.0 is a harder, better-verified 89-task set; 2.1 (2026-05-06) fixed 28 tasks and added continuous validation.
task_source: Hand-curated tasks inspired by real terminal workflows, community-contributed and reviewer-verified; each task ships a container environment plus a programmatic checker (Harbor framework, github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench).
metric: Task resolution rate (fraction of tasks whose verification script passes). Terminal-Bench 2.0 leader as of July 2026: GPT-5.5 at 0.827 across 49 evaluated models (llm-stats.com/benchmarks/terminal-bench-2).
contamination_status: Tasks are bespoke (not scraped from public issue trackers), which limits pretraining leakage but not post-release overfitting; the project runs an explicit anti-cheating/reward-hacking policy for the leaderboard (announced 2026-04-19).
maintenance_state: active — 2.1 released 2026-05-06; Terminal-Bench 3.0 call for contributions 2026-03-05; Harbor-Index spinoff 2026-07-06; Terminal-Bench Challenges (long-horizon single-task) 2026-06-18.
harness_lessons: The 2.0-to-2.1 revision (28 of 89 tasks fixed after release) shows that verifier scripts are the benchmark, and they rot: continuous validation of checkers is as important as the tasks themselves. Harbor's separation of agent, environment, and verifier is the reference architecture for rolling your own terminal eval. The explicit reward-hacking policy is a reminder that any pass/fail oracle an agent can inspect will eventually be gamed.
notes: Family now spans four artifacts: core benchmark, Harbor (harness), Harbor-Index (lightweight diverse subset), and Terminal-Bench Challenges (token-intensive long-horizon single tasks). zai-org/terminal-bench-2-verified on Hugging Face mirrors the verified task set. News timeline: 1.0 2025-05-19, 2.0 + Harbor 2025-11-07, 2.1 2026-05-06 (tbench.ai/news).
